raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded proteins, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR). It has shifted from a rare post-mortem diagnosis to a treatable, increasingly recognized cause of heart failure, arrhythmia, conduction disease, and aortic stenosis phenocopies. Contemporary consensus documents emphasize early suspicion, precise amyloid typing, multidisciplinary care, and rapid initiation of disease-modifying therapy [1], [2], [3], [4]. AL amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency because circulating light chains may exert direct cardiotoxicity and survival is strongly determined by cardiac involvement, whereas ATTR cardiomyopathy reflects deposition of either wild-type transthyretin, typically in older adults, or variant transthyretin due to pathogenic TTR mutations [2], [3], [5].

Clinical “red flags” include unexplained increased left ventricular wall thickness, heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis, atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular block, autonomic dysfunction, proteinuria, peripheral neuropathy, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, macroglossia, and periorbital purpura. Electrocardiographic low voltage is helpful when present but insensitive; discordance between wall thickness and QRS voltage remains classic. Echocardiography commonly shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve/interatrial septal thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced global longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [6]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance provides characteristic diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume; late gadolinium enhancement patterns also carry prognostic information [7], [8].

Diagnosis requires both confirmation of amyloid and identification of amyloid type. All suspected patients should undergo serum free light-chain assay plus serum and urine immunofixation to evaluate for a monoclonal process. If monoclonal testing is abnormal, tissue confirmation and typing—preferably by mass spectrometry—are essential because ATTR and monoclonal gammopathy may coexist. In the absence of monoclonal protein, grade 2–3 myocardial uptake on bone-avid scintigraphy with technetium-labeled PYP, DPD, or HMDP can diagnose ATTR cardiomyopathy non-invasively [9], [10]. Abdominal fat aspiration has high sensitivity in AL but much lower sensitivity in ATTR, so a negative result does not exclude cardiac disease [11]. Once ATTR is diagnosed, TTR genetic testing distinguishes wild-type from variant disease and guides family screening.

Epidemiology is context-dependent. ATTR wild-type explains a meaningful minority of older patients hospitalized with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and increased wall thickness [12]. Coexisting ATTR is also found in severe calcific aortic stenosis, including patients undergoing surgical valve replacement and transcatheter aortic valve replacement, where it may worsen functional status and prognosis [13], [14]. Musculoskeletal manifestations can precede cardiomyopathy by years; amyloid deposits in tenosynovial tissue at carpal tunnel release provide an opportunity for earlier recognition [15].

Risk stratification integrates symptoms, biomarkers, renal function, imaging, and amyloid type. In AL, troponin and NT-proBNP form the backbone of Mayo staging, refined by the difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains [16], [17]. In ATTR, staging systems using NT-proBNP, troponin, and estimated glomerular filtration rate predict survival and help contextualize treatment benefit [18], [19]. Serial assessment should include functional class, diuretic needs, rhythm and conduction evaluation, renal function, biomarkers, and disease-specific hematologic or transthyretin measures.

Management has two parallel aims: supportive cardiac care and suppression or stabilization of the amyloid precursor. Loop diuretics are central for congestion, but patients often tolerate vasodilators, beta-blockers, and renin–angiotensin inhibitors poorly because of restrictive physiology and autonomic dysfunction. Atrial fibrillation is common; anticoagulation thresholds are often lower than in non-amyloid cardiomyopathy because atrial mechanical dysfunction and thrombus may occur despite controlled rhythm. Pacemakers are used for standard indications, while defibrillator benefit is individualized.

For AL amyloidosis, therapy targets the plasma-cell clone and should begin urgently after typing. Bortezomib-based cyclophosphamide-bortezomib-dexamethasone improved hematologic responses, but advanced cardiac AL remains high risk [20]. Daratumumab added to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone increased complete hematologic responses and organ-progression–free survival in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [21]. Hematologic and organ responses should be monitored using consensus criteria [30]. Selected patients may undergo autologous stem-cell transplantation, but cardiac involvement often limits eligibility.

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis established transthyretin stabilization as disease-modifying therapy by reducing mortality, cardiovascular hospitalizations, and decline in function and quality of life; long-term extension data support earlier treatment [22], [23]. Acoramidis, another transthyretin stabilizer, improved a hierarchical composite outcome in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24]. Gene-silencing approaches reduce hepatic transthyretin production: patisiran improved neuropathy and cardiac parameters in hereditary ATTR and later preserved functional capacity in ATTR cardiomyopathy [25], [26], [27]; vutrisiran reduced death and cardiovascular events in ATTR cardiomyopathy [28]. Inotersen benefits hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy but requires platelet and renal monitoring [29]. The therapeutic landscape therefore increasingly rewards early diagnosis before irreversible myocardial remodeling.
